definition: A language and a group of peoples of south-western Nigeria, Benin and Togo, with related communities across the Atlantic world. Yoruba religion, Ifá divination and the orisha are shared across these communities, though practice varies greatly.

Divine beings who serve Olodumare and are approached through ritual, offering and possession. Each has a distinct character, domain, colour and shrine. The number is often given as 401, meaning many, and the term is spelled orisa in Yoruba.
The supreme being in Yoruba tradition, also called Olorun or Eleda, who is the source of life and of ase. Olodumare is not counted among the orisha and is often approached through them.

A system of divination and an oral literary corpus, performed by trained babalawos. Its chapters, called odu, contain stories, proverbs and prescriptions. Ifá is learned through apprenticeship and ritual, not from a single public book.

The orisha of crossroads, messages, chance and exchange, who carries offerings between humans and the other orisha. He is a trickster who tests pride and exposes partial views. He is not the devil of Christian tradition.

The orisha of iron, tools, roads, hunting and war, honoured by blacksmiths, farmers, hunters and drivers. He opens the way and also embodies the danger of unchecked force, so his power is bound by oath and taboo.
The orisha of the Osun River and of sweet water, fertility, love, beauty and wealth. Her worship centres on the river and grove at Osogbo, and she is associated with brass, honey and yellow cloth.

The orisha of thunder and lightning and the remembered king of Oyo, associated with justice, the double-headed axe and bata drumming. His story is told differently in different towns, and oaths are sworn on his name.

The city in south-western Nigeria that Yoruba tradition honours as the place where dry land first spread and where human beings were shaped. It is the seat of the Ooni and a major ritual centre, with many shrines.

The power or authority that makes words, actions and rituals effective, ultimately from Olodumare. Ase is present in blessings, curses, medicines and divination, and it is affirmed in the phrase ase, so be it.
